subject: RFP: uptime & latency validation playbook, measurement methodology and credit timeline

Oliver — thank you for the questionnaire. We reviewed and attached our formal responses (Redwood_SLO_Response_20260923.pdf) and a concise Measurement Playbook (Measurement_Playbook.xlsx) that outlines data sources, sampling cadence, and exclusion criteria. High-level answers to your two asks:

- Measurement source: primary signal is the Redwood control plane aggregated at per-tenant granularity (ingestion and response success/latency derived from routed inference requests). We also provide optional dedicated in-region synthetic probes for customers who require an independent probe layer. The control plane is our source-of-truth for contractual SLOs.

- Credit claims: Customers submit a credit request via our portal (link included in the attached doc). Claims must be filed within 30 calendar days of the end of the affected billing month. We validate against stored telemetry, incident timelines, and any agreed maintenance windows; validation commonly completes within 14 business days, and credits (if applicable) are applied to the next billing cycle.

Some specific SLO commitments included in the response:
- Hosted Redwood API: monthly uptime SLO 99.95% (excludes agreed maintenance windows).
- Dedicated (reserved capacity): monthly uptime SLO 99.9% with higher-tier latency SLOs configurable by contract.
- Latency SLOs: we publish p50/p95/p99 tail-latency targets per model class and route; contract language pins the applicable percentile and sequence-length buckets.

Measurement methodology (summary): rolling monthly window, 30s sampling resolution for availability checks derived from request success/HTTP status and application-level timeouts; latency uses tokenized-response timing with sequence-length normalization. The Measurement_Playbook.xlsx provides exact formulas and example calculations.

I've cc'd our technical and legal leads for any detailed follow-ups. Happy to set a short sync if you want to walk through the playbook line-by-line.

Best,

From: Sean Gallagher <sean.gallagher@redwood.com>

Subject: Re: Fwd: RFP: uptime & latency validation playbook — internal clarifications

Hannah — quick tech clarifications to back the playbook we sent. Highlights below; I'll attach a short notes file with explicit formulas.

- Telemetry retention: primary raw request logs are retained for 180 days in our central telemetry store; aggregated SLO metrics and histograms are retained for 24 months. The 90-day number in the draft was conservative; update to 180 days if we want to be precise.

- Measurement logic: availability is computed per-tenant as: 1 - (failed_requests / total_requests) over a rolling 30-day window by default for operational dashboards; contractual monthly SLOs use a calendar-month window unless a different window is specified in the SOW. We sample at 30s resolution for synthetic probes and derive per-request success from both HTTP status and downstream model runtime completion code.

- Exclusions: planned maintenance windows require >= 7 days notice and must be < 4 hours per calendar month to be auto-excluded. Emergency maintenance (security patches, critical infra) can be excluded with a post-facto notice and incident report.

- Tail-latency and fallback: for latency SLOs we normalize across sequence length by bucketing common sequence-length ranges; p99 tail-latency violations are computed within the applicable bucket. Automatic fallback (model variant downgrade) triggers when median token-time exceeds the configured threshold or when KV cache warm-up fails; fallback events are recorded and surfaced in the incident timeline but do not count as planned maintenance.

- Dispute evidence: telemetry snapshots, request traces (sampled up to configurable rate per tenant), and control-plane routing logs are retained and signed by our audit pipeline. We can provide signed audit extracts for credit disputes.

Attached: slo_measurement_notes.txt (plain text with formulas and example calculations). Happy to hop on a 30-min call with EnterpriseCorp to walk through examples.

— Sean

All — quick legal/ops confirmation to close the loop before we send the final RFP package to EnterpriseCorp:

- Maintenance notice: 7 days is acceptable for standard maintenance. Emergency maintenance language will reference our incident management process and will be limited to critical security patches.
- Credit claims: 30-day filing window from month-end, 14 business day validation period, and credits applied to the following invoice cycle is acceptable. We'll include a short SLA exhibit in the SOW with these timelines and a simple table that maps monthly uptime percentage to credit % (example ranges in attached SLACredit_Process.md).
- Escalation path: claims escalate from AM -> Legal -> CTO on a 5-business-day cadence if unresolved. We'll include a single-point contact and a 30-day final arbitration window (mutual agreement) in enterprise contracts.

Please confirm any last-minute objections; otherwise I'll package the final response and send to EnterpriseCorp Monday morning.

Thanks,
